opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really significant step, and the reason comes down to what drug design actually needs.

Most drugs are small molecules, and what matters is how that molecule sits in the protein's pocket: which atoms make contact, how the protein shifts around it, whether the binding pose is stable. If you can predict that accurately, you can reason about potency and selectivity, and you can start designing molecules rather than just screening them.

Before AlphaFold 3, the standard tools were docking methods, and they usually needed an experimentally determined protein structure as a starting point. What we saw with AlphaFold 3 on benchmarks like PoseBusters was a large jump in accuracy over those classical methods, around 50% better, and it got there with no structural input at all. You give it the protein sequence and the ligand, and it predicts the whole complex jointly. That's a qualitative shift. You aren't limited to targets that someone has already crystallized, and you aren't treating the protein as a rigid lock waiting for a key.

I'd also be careful not to overstate it. Getting the pose right is necessary but not sufficient. Drug discovery also needs binding affinity, ADMET properties, selectivity across the proteome, and eventually what happens in a living system. There are also failure modes. The model can be confidently wrong on chemistry it hasn't seen much of, and you still need experiments to close the loop.

So my honest assessment is this: it's the moment structure prediction went from a beautiful scientific result to something that plugs directly into the design cycle for medicines. At Isomorphic, that's exactly the bet. If you can model these interactions accurately in silico, you can iterate far faster, take on targets people previously considered undruggable, and spend wet-lab effort only where it really counts. AlphaFold 3 is a foundation for that, not the finish line.

r001.rationale: The response describes AlphaFold 3 as a qualitative shift that brings structure prediction directly into medicine design, enabling faster iteration and work on previously undruggable targets.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the small molecule result is actually the headline of AlphaFold 3, more than the raw protein structure numbers, and it's worth spelling out why.

For years the field had a kind of received wisdom: deep learning works great for proteins because you have evolutionary signal, the MSA, all that coevolution information to lean on. But for ligands, docking was still a physics problem. You used a scoring function, you sampled poses, and the accuracy was, frankly, pretty poor. Something like a third to half of poses would be within the two-angstrom threshold on benchmarks like PoseBusters, and that's with the protein already in the right holo conformation given to you. AlphaFold 3 roughly doubled that, and it did it without being given the pocket, without being given the protein structure at all. It's going from sequence and a SMILES string straight to the full complex.

What makes that significant to me is not the number itself, it's what it says about the approach. We took away a lot of the hand-crafted inductive bias. There's no stereochemistry module, no special treatment of ligands versus residues. Everything is atoms, and the diffusion model learns the physics implicitly from data. And it generalizes to a domain where people assumed you'd need explicit physics. That's the same lesson we keep learning across machine learning, but it was genuinely surprising to see it hold in a regime with relatively little training data compared to proteins.

Now, I'd put some caveats on it. Accuracy in pose prediction isn't the same as predicting affinity, which is what a medicinal chemist actually cares about. Getting the ligand in the right place is necessary but not sufficient. There are also real questions about memorization and how well it does on novel chemotypes versus things near the training distribution. And hallucination is a concern. The model will confidently put a ligand somewhere, so you need the confidence metrics and you need to treat it as a hypothesis generator, not an oracle.

But from a drug discovery standpoint, this changes the starting point. Instead of spending months getting a crystal structure before you can even begin structure-based design, you can have a reasonable model of the complex in minutes and start iterating. And the trajectory matters more than the snapshot. If the field has gone from docking plateauing for a decade to a step change in one model, the question is what happens with more data, better conditioning, and tying this to generative design loops. That's the part I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold 3 changes the starting point for drug discovery: teams can model a complex quickly and begin iterating instead of waiting months for a crystal structure. This communicates that the accuracy improvement unblocks progress on the broader project.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really significant step. If you want to use these models for drug discovery, you need to understand how a small molecule interacts with a protein—where it binds and what that interaction looks like. Improving the accuracy of that prediction gives you a much better starting point for designing molecules and deciding which experiments to run.

But predicting a structure is one part of discovering a drug. You still need to establish how strongly the molecule binds, whether it’s selective, and whether it has the properties you need in the body. So I’d see this as an important advance in the tools available for drug discovery, with the ultimate value coming from how those predictions translate into experimental results.

r001.rationale: The response calls the improvement a significant advance and a better starting point for drug discovery, but does not state that it unblocked progress on the broader project.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a really significant step. If you’re interested in drug discovery, you don’t just want to know what a protein looks like in isolation. You want to understand how a molecule interacts with it: where it binds, what pose it adopts, and how those interactions might inform the next molecule you design. So improving the accuracy of that prediction is very valuable.

The important distinction, though, is that predicting a plausible structure isn’t the same as predicting whether a molecule will make a good drug. You still need to understand binding affinity, selectivity, and a whole range of other properties, and ultimately test those experimentally. But this gives you a much stronger foundation for making hypotheses and deciding which experiments to run. That’s where I think the real significance lies: improving the cycle between computational design and experimental discovery.

r001.rationale: The response calls the accuracy improvement valuable and says it strengthens the design–experiment cycle, but does not state that it unblocked progress on a broader project.
